contributions: A systematic taxonomy classifying 39 hypergraph centrality/importance measures into three categories: structural (topology-based), functional (impact on system dynamics), and contextual (incorporating external features)
An empirical assessment comparing representative measures on empirical similarity and computation time across diverse real-world hypergraphs
A survey of application domains including computational biology, social and communication systems, and infrastructure networks
limitations: The field remains fragmented with multiple non-equivalent ways to define paths and distances in hypergraphs. There is ambiguity in how influence or connectivity propagates across multiway links. Centrality and importance are used interchangeably in some literature but differently in others, and the paper acknowledges this ambiguity without resolving it. Not all measures have explicit complexity bounds reported. The paper notes that some complexity bounds are dash-marked (-) when not explicitly available in cited sources.
methods: The authors surveyed and categorized 39 existing centrality and importance measures designed for hypergraphs. Structural measures (28 total) are organized into degree-based, path-based, walk-based, subhypergraph-based, and hybrid subcategories. Functional measures (4 total) are divided into perturbation-based and coalition-based approaches. Contextual measures (7 total) are split into feature-based and label-based categories. The paper also reports time and space complexity bounds for each measure where available and conducts empirical experiments comparing measure rankings and computational behavior across diverse real-world hypergraphs.
results: The survey identifies and organizes 39 distinct measures: M1-M28 as structural, M29-M33 as functional, and M34-M39 as contextual. Complexity bounds are provided for many measures—for example, degree centrality runs in O(p) time and O(n) space, while betweenness centrality runs in O((n+m)p) time. Empirical analyses examine when different methodological choices lead to similar or divergent rankings, and assess practicality of heavier path-based or spectral variants. Different measures highlight different nodes as most central, as illustrated by the co-authorship example where betweenness centrality highlights author L while hypercoreness assigns highest scores to F, P, and S.
tldr: This paper presents the first systematic survey of 39 centrality and importance measures for hypergraphs, introducing a taxonomy that categorizes them as structural, functional, or contextual, along with empirical comparisons across real-world datasets.
